entities.name: African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The African Methodist Episcopal Zion Church (AME Zion), founded in 1796 in New York City by James Varick and other free Black Methodists who separated from the segregated John Street Methodist Church, is one of the oldest and most historically significant African American Christian denominations — known as 'the Freedom Church' because of its deep roots in the abolitionist movement and the fact that Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, and Sojourner Truth were all members or associated with AME Zion congregations.

AME Zion was established because Black Methodists in New York were denied full participation in white Methodist congregations — they could not preach, vote on church matters, or receive communion at the same table. James Varick led the effort to establish an independent African Methodist congregation, incorporated in 1801 and receiving its first bishop in 1822. The denomination spread throughout the Northern states and, after the Civil War, rapidly expanded into the South among newly freed enslaved people.

The denomination's association with Frederick Douglass (who lectured and preached from AME Zion pulpits), Harriet Tubman (a devoted member who received church support for her Underground Railroad activities), and Sojourner Truth made it synonymous with Black freedom and dignity in 19th-century America. Today AME Zion has approximately 1.4 million members, primarily in the United States, with congregations in Africa, the Caribbean, and Europe. It remains an active voice in African American civic and religious life.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: AME Zion — the 'Freedom Church' founded by free Black New Yorkers, associated with Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, and Sojourner Truth, and a foundational institution of African American spiritual and civic independence — is one of the most historically significant Black Christian denominations in American history.
